title: Judge halts Army’s plan to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making material as Iowa residents worry about lead exposure | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

A federal judge has ordered the US Army to pause its plans to detonate five tons of lead azide on Monday after environmental activists filed a lawsuit expressing concerns about the potential impacts of the explosion.

Officials at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, in coordination with the US Environmental Protection Agency, planned to destroy 68 drums oflead azide, a material used to detonate munitions, the Army said.

The detonation in the southeastern town of Middletown was initially scheduled for Friday but waspostponed to Mondayafter pushback from the public and elected officials.

“I have heard from many Iowans who are worried about their health and safety due to the potential risk of lead exposure as a result of the detonation,” Senator-elect Josh Turek said Thursday in calling for a delay.

But the three-day delay didn’t calm the nerves of Lucy Giehl, who lives just 4 miles north of the ammunition plant.

“What are they going to do during those three days to help people be better prepared?” Giehl openly wondered toThe Associated Press. “There’s just so many details that I feel like haven’t been addressed with the public.”

Sue Dyer, who owns a 1,200-acre farm of corn and beans about 18 miles west of the Army facility, said she is frustrated with the lack of communication, as she only found out about the detonation a few days ago.

“I mean, there’s lots of cattle around there, even pets, people,” she told CNN. “If this stuff deposits lead all over everything, what the heck are we supposed to do? We’re just going to be poisoned every day.”

The Army, in a joint statement with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA, said Friday afternoon, “The entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa is conducted in the safest fashion possible.”

“Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” the statement said, adding they will keep local officials and the public updated.

The judge’s order does not say when the court will take further action on the case, but the EPA said in a court filing they planned to file a response by November 22.

Environmental advocates in a news briefing on Friday called on state leaders, including Gov. Kim Reynolds, to take control of communication over the potential detonation.

The federal government, including the Army and EPA, couldn’t be trusted to adequately inform Iowans about risks of the planned detonation, Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, told reporters.

“Iowans deserve a transparent, coordinated, and effective response to this unprecedented event,” Schmidt said.

Reynolds’ office announced Friday afternoon they launched the State Emergency Operations Center to coordinate state agencies with the Army and EPA regarding the detonation.

CNN has reached out to Reynolds’ office for comment.

Lead azide is a volatile lead compound that can “explode from shock, heat, flame or friction when dry,” according to a federalhazardous materials database.

“Extensive modeling efforts predict that the potential level of lead particles in the air may be elevated,” the Army said. “The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground.”

Lead is toxic to the brain, andno amount of exposure is considered safe. But it’s unclear how much lead might be released into the environment after the detonation.

Lead is heavier than air, so it will be limited in how far it can travel, said Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a University of Iowa professor and environmental health expert.

Any sizable particles would likely land within 20 miles of the detonation – “and then it’s only going to be the much, much smaller ones that will maintain themselves lofted with the wind and move down, downwind … towards Iowa City,” he told CNN.

O’Shaughnessy said he and colleagues plan to test and monitor the air and ground to see how much fallout there could be.

In addition to possible lead exposure, loud noises and ground vibrations from the detonation could cause “localized window damage,” the Army said.

Daren Paul Morris, who walks his dog near the Army ammunition plant every day, toldCNN affiliate KCRGhe plans to evacuate. But he’s worried about what fallout he’ll come home to – both visible and invisible.

“Hopefully I don’t have any broken windows. I just had the roof replaced,” Morris said.

“I don’t know if I would mow the grass for the first time until it rained good. You know you don’t want to kick up all that dust,” he added. “They haven’t really told us how toxic … well, lead is obviously toxic.”

Keara Puetz is one of the many Iowans who learned of the now-halted detonation from somewhere other than her local government, saying she saw it on the news.

“I couldn’t really believe what I was seeing,” said the lifelong Iowan, who comes from a line of farmers. She hopes the pause will help clarify important questions her family has.

“Like if we need help with cleaning our crops, who’s going to help clean them?” she asked. “How are we gonna clean our crops, our soil, or what’s the next steps?”

Jen Rowray, who lives in a rural area of eastern Iowa, said she is also worried about the long-term effects of the lead.

“We are very aware of how much the soil can be affected by a heavy metal like lead that doesn’t really go away,” she told CNN. “I mean, it can disperse. It can go a little lower … we’re very aware how can it get literally into the vegetables we eat, root vegetables suck up the nutrients, and it’s going to pull that up.”

Iowa also has the second-highest cancer rate of any US state,CNN previously reported. It’s only one of three states where the rate is rising.

Schmidt said Iowa’s demographics and residents’ behavioral factors don’t fully explain the state’s high cancer rates. Instead, he cited Iowa Environmental Council’sMarch reportthat suggested residents face additional environmental risk factors that contribute to increased prevalence of cancer among the population. He pointed to Muscatine County, about 50 north of the Army’s Middletown plant, which already has higher lead emissions.

“This is just adding another layer of environmental pollution, putting people’s health at risk,” he said.

Rowray said there needs to be an outside expert who can come in and give a second opinion.

While she understands this is an urgent problem that needs to be taken care of, she doesn’t trust the Army’s opinion, given their lack of communication, and would like to have more information, she said.

“I think we have the right also to be concerned about that drift, that plume,” Rowray said. “But as soon as possible doesn’t mean a rush through to where the, the public is losing trust because they’re not getting the right information, and they’re not getting like guidance that seems to make sense.”

Environmental advocates said residents received little notice from the Army about the potential detonation.

Schmidt questioned whether the lead azide instability was a new problem that required immediate detonation.

“The Army found out about it many months ago, and then provided residents with a five-day notice,” he said. “I think there could have been a lot of different decisions and steps leading up to this.”

In March, the Army discovered the degrading lead azide “housed in bunkers at the installation” and immediately started communicating with stakeholders and residents “about the danger it posed,” Acting US Army Secretary Adam Telle said.

In the months that followed, the Army worked to develop “a scientifically validated, fully coordinated safety plan before engaging the public,” officials said.

After coordinating with the EPA, experts and the community, officials determined a controlled detonation “posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area,” Telle said.

That’s because the lead azide’s degraded status has left it “extremely unstable and sensitive to even slight friction or movement” — meaning relocating the material could be more dangerous, the Army said in a flyer distributed to the community last month.

“Packing and transporting it poses an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation to personnel handling and transporting as well as to the public,” the flyer says.

But waiting too long to detonate the lead azide could pose more hazards later, Telle said. He previously said Monday would be the “latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”

Theemergency permitfrom the EPA, which went into effect starting November 13, 2026, and goes through February 11, 2027, allows the Army to do the detonation in that period.

The cleanup requirements under the current permit are inadequate to properly address the scope and degree of potential impacts, Thien Chau, a senior attorney at the environmental advocacy nonprofit Earthjustice, said.

He added there doesn’t appear to be sufficient understanding of how far the plume would spread, as well as which bodies of water, such as the Mississippi River, and land would be blanketed with lead dust, including where people live.

Portions of western Illinois, just across the Mississippi River from Iowa, are currently included inmodeling showing possible exposureto lead dust from the blast.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said Friday afternoon that he had spoken with Telle to “to urge more transparency” on the planned detonation.

“The State is still seeking more data from them on how this could impact Illinoisans and is working to keep you informed and safe,” he said.

Illinois health and environmental protection officials said they are monitoring the potential detonation and have issued updates to residents.

“There is no safe level of lead in the body, and when inhaled or swallowed, it can pose serious health risks,” Dr. Sameer Vohra, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, said in astatement.

Illinois officials listed a number of safety tips, such as staying indoors and keeping windows closed for 24 to 48 hours after detonation; washing hands before eating and drinking; and taking shoes off when entering homes to minimize tracking of contaminants.

CNN’s Kara Devlin, Bill Kirkos and Nic Anderson contributed to this report.

Correction:A previous version of this story misstated Iowa resident Keara Puetz’s last name and her job description. She is a fertility advocate.
